title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 65–66
description: Curated B2 addition linkers and text-referring language for coherent explanations, arguments and problem–solution writing.

units.title: Unit 65 — Addition
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 136–137 (PDF pages 137–138).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose sentence-linking expressions for addition according to formality and emphasis.
Use end-of-sentence expressions to extend lists and emphasise an extra quality.
Combine clauses, noun phrases and -ing forms accurately after addition expressions.
Distinguish academic or business-writing linkers from conversational alternatives.

items.example: The equipment is reliable. In addition, it is easy to maintain.
items.note: Often starts a new sentence or clause, with a comma; suitable in formal and neutral writing.

items.example: The course covers electronics. Additionally, it includes practical laboratory work.
items.note: Similar to in addition; often used in reports, presentations and formal emails.

items.example: The device is expensive. Furthermore, it requires specialist training.
items.note: Formal linker adding another supporting point; broadly interchangeable with moreover.

items.example: The proposal lacks detail. Moreover, its costs are difficult to estimate.
items.note: Relatively formal, especially when building a written argument.

items.pt: além do mais; e tem mais
items.example: The hotel is close to the station. What's more, breakfast is included.
items.note: Conversational and informal; introduces an especially appealing or significant extra point.

items.example: The application is secure. What is more, it has a simple interface.
items.note: The uncontracted form is relatively formal compared with what's more; may sound emphatic.

items.example: Clear instructions are important. Equally, staff need time to practise.
items.note: Adds a point of comparable importance, often while arguing or weighing ideas; not a general-purpose synonym of furthermore.

items.example: The morning team met its deadline. Likewise, the evening team finished on time.
items.note: Adds a similar or corresponding fact, response or opinion.

items.pt: além de tudo isso; para completar
items.example: The car broke down. On top of all that, it started pouring with rain.
items.note: Emphatic and mostly informal, especially in speech; all can be omitted: on top of that.

items.example: The job offers flexible hours plus opportunities to travel.
items.note: Normally joins noun phrases; informal speech also uses plus to connect clauses.

items.example: We discussed staffing, equipment, deadlines and so on.
items.note: Informal way to leave a list open; common in speech and ordinary writing.

items.example: Bring paper, pencils, rulers, et cetera.
items.note: Usually written as etc.; slightly more formal than and so on. The spoken form is et cetera.

items.word: and so on and so forth
items.pt: e assim por diante; e por aí vai
items.example: First came the interviews, then the paperwork, and so on and so forth.
items.note: Informal, sometimes implying a tiresome or lengthy sequence; keep this fixed word order.

items.example: She is an excellent organiser and a talented designer into the bargain.
items.note: Informal expression usually placed at the end to emphasise an additional characteristic.

items.example: The flat is spacious, affordable and close to the park to boot.
items.note: Informal emphatic expression generally placed at the end; not normally used to introduce a sentence.

items.pt: em referência a; dando continuidade a
items.example: Further to our conversation on Tuesday, I am sending the updated figures.
items.note: Formal correspondence opener referring to a previous message, call or discussion; followed by a noun phrase.

items.example: In addition to supervising the team, she writes technical documentation.
items.note: Follow with a noun phrase or verb + -ing, not a complete finite clause.

items.pt: além de; paralelamente a; ao lado de
items.example: Alongside his research, he teaches an evening class.
items.note: Adds an activity or responsibility carried out in parallel; followed by a noun phrase or -ing form.

items.example: As well as reviewing the design, he checked the test results.
items.note: In this construction, use a noun or -ing form, not a finite clause such as as well as he reviewed.

items.example: Besides working full-time, she is studying for a qualification.
items.note: Introduces an additional consideration; followed by a noun or verb + -ing in this pattern.

items.example: Apart from learning French, he is taking a photography course.
items.note: Can mean besides or except depending on the context; followed by a noun phrase or -ing form.

items.example: The director arrived along with two visiting researchers.
items.note: Connects people, things or accompanying circumstances; takes a noun phrase or -ing form.

items.example: Her experience, together with her qualifications, makes her a strong candidate.
items.note: Adds an accompanying factor; the verb normally agrees with the main subject, not the added phrase.

units.title: Unit 66 — Referring words
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 138–139 (PDF pages 139–140).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Use general referring nouns to connect ideas across sentences and organise an argument.
Differentiate issues, claims, facts, viewpoints, questions, topics and aspects.
Use problem–solution vocabulary with accurate prepositions and natural collocations.
Select words for situations, responses, solutions and evaluations in formal discussion.

items.pt: palavras de referência textual; termos que retomam ideias
items.example: Text-referring words help readers connect a statement with an earlier idea.
items.note: A linguistic label for general nouns whose specific meaning depends on the surrounding text.

items.example: The server keeps disconnecting. This problem needs urgent attention.
items.note: Refers back to a difficulty already described; helps avoid repeating the whole explanation.

items.example: Several teams suggested ways to save energy, but no solution was agreed.
items.note: A way of dealing successfully with a problem; typical phrase: solution to a problem.

items.pt: questão; assunto controverso; problema em debate
items.example: Whether to introduce new fees remains a divisive issue.
items.note: A topic involving debate, concern or controversy; less specific than a question needing a factual answer.

items.pt: questão; pergunta; problema a ser respondido
items.example: Whether the treatment is safe is still an unanswered question.
items.note: Refers to something to investigate or answer; not every question is a controversial issue.

items.example: Renewable energy is the main topic of today's discussion.
items.note: A general subject discussed in a conversation, debate, essay or presentation.

items.pt: aspecto; faceta; parte de um assunto
items.example: The report examines the economic aspect of the proposed changes.
items.note: Refers to one particular part or feature of a broader subject; aspect of something.

items.example: The company rejected the claim that its equipment was unsafe.
items.note: An assertion that may be disputed; a claim is not necessarily established as a fact.

items.example: The figures confirm one fact: demand has increased sharply.
items.note: A verifiable piece of information, unlike an opinion or an unsupported claim.

items.example: Her main argument is that public transport should be more affordable.
items.note: A reasoned case supporting a point of view; can also mean a disagreement in everyday speech.

items.example: The key point is that the equipment must remain accessible.
items.note: Refers to the central idea or a particular detail in a discussion.

items.example: Our position is that all participants should have equal access.
items.note: Here position means a publicly held opinion or policy; distinct from one's circumstances.

items.example: I respect her view, even though I disagree with her conclusion.
items.note: An opinion or perspective; useful for referring back to a stated stance.

items.example: The situation has become more difficult since funding was reduced.
items.note: Refers broadly to the current state of a problem or set of circumstances.

items.example: The lack of trained staff is a worrying state of affairs.
items.note: More formal phrase for how things currently stand; often negative or evaluative.

items.example: The organisation is now in a difficult financial position.
items.note: This sense refers to the circumstances of a person or group, not an expressed opinion.

items.pt: em relação a; no que diz respeito a
items.example: We need to clarify our position with regard to data protection.
items.note: Formal phrase indicating the topic or area concerned; also common in business correspondence.

items.example: Traffic congestion causes delays across the city every morning.
items.note: Often used with traffic and urban transport; a specific problem requiring a response.

items.example: The committee faced a dilemma over whether to raise fees or cut services.
items.note: A difficult situation involving competing choices or undesirable alternatives.

items.example: The main difficulty lies in finding qualified staff.
items.note: A somewhat more formal alternative to problem; common with difficulty in doing something.

items.example: The shortage developed into a serious housing crisis.
items.note: A major or urgent problem, stronger than a routine difficulty; plural crises.

items.example: The missing documents are a matter we need to resolve immediately.
items.note: General term for a situation that needs attention or discussion; not always serious.

items.example: The council's response to the complaints was to extend opening hours.
items.note: Often denotes deliberate action or communication in reply to a problem; response to something.

items.example: Her immediate reaction to the proposal was surprise.
items.note: Often describes an instinctive or emotional response; reaction to something.

items.example: His attitude to remote work has changed considerably.
items.note: An opinion or way of thinking about something; attitude to is a typical British pattern.

items.example: We need a different approach to reducing energy consumption.
items.note: A method for tackling an issue; approach to + noun or -ing form.

items.example: A new timetable might be the answer to our scheduling difficulties.
items.note: In problem–solution writing, answer to means a possible way of solving a problem.

items.example: Both sides worked towards a peaceful resolution to the dispute.
items.note: Often used for settling disagreements or problems; resolution to or resolution of is possible depending on context.

items.example: Better communication may be the key to improving safety.
items.note: Figurative phrase the key to + noun or -ing form; identifies the most important factor.

items.example: The negotiators are looking for a way out of the dispute.
items.note: Fixed pattern: a way out of a problem, crisis or difficult situation.

items.example: An independent evaluation of the programme will be published soon.
items.note: Describes judging how well a solution or policy worked; evaluation of something.

items.example: The experts' assessment of the risks was more cautious than ours.
items.note: An informed judgement of a situation, proposal or outcome; assessment of something.

items.example: Her professional judgement was that the project should continue.
items.note: A considered opinion or decision; judgement is a British spelling, and judgment is also used.

items.example: His belief that people can change shapes his teaching style.
items.note: Refers to something a person accepts as true, whether or not it can be proved.

items.example: The committee is still deciding whether the proposal is viable.
items.note: Describes an approach or solution that can realistically work.

items.example: The reason for the strange signal remains a mystery.
items.note: A question or event not yet explained; related to the open-question language in the exercises.

items.example: The available evidence does not support the original claim.
items.note: Uncountable in this sense; evidence supports or challenges claims rather than merely restating a view.
